lessons.title: Ich putze mir die Zähne: mich or mir?
lessons.goal: Choose mir or dir when the sentence already has a body part as object, and tell what happened to Frau Weber with sich or mir and the Perfekt.

grammar.topic: Reflexive pronouns: accusative or dative (mich or mir)
grammar.point: A reflexive pronoun is accusative when there is no other object (Ich wasche mich). If the sentence already has an accusative object, such as a body part, the pronoun becomes dative: Ich wasche mir die Hände. Only ich and du change (mir, dir); sich, uns and euch stay the same.

mistake.why: The hands are already the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun must be dative: mir.

terms.meaning: the small word that points back to the subject: mich, mir, sich
mir or dir, used when the sentence already has an accusative object
a word like Zähne, Hände or Knöchel that stands as the object after mir or dir

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich wasche mich' to 'Ich wasche mir die Hände'
cards.body: This chapter is called Rund um Körper und Geist (body and mind): hospital, health, learning and music. Today starts with the body. On Saturday morning Frau Weber falls on the stairs. To tell what happened to her, you need one tiny change: mich becomes mir.
steps: You already know: Ich fühle mich gut. The words mich, dich and sich from A2 chapter 4 point back to the person who acts.
New today: Ich putze mir die Zähne. When the sentence already has another object, ich and du use mir and dir.
By the end you can: say what you do to your own body and tell what happened to Frau Weber.

examples.de: Ich fühle mich gut.
examples.en: I feel good.
examples.why: You know this already: mich points back to ich.

examples.de: Ich putze mir die Zähne.
examples.en: I brush my teeth.
examples.why: New today: the teeth are the object, so mich becomes mir.

cards.more: Think of a small word that works like a mirror. Mich and mir both mean: me, myself. German keeps two versions because of a simple question: is there already something else in the sentence that I am doing something to? If not, you use mich. If yes, for example my teeth or my hands, you use mir. Only ich and du change. Everything else stays the same. We take it slowly, one card at a time, with Frau Weber's Saturday as our story.

cards.title: Saturday morning: Frau Weber falls on the stairs
cards.body: On Saturday morning Frau Weber falls on the stairs of the house. Mira and Leon are there. Read the short scene in the steps. Look for two little words: sich and mir. They are reflexive pronouns: they point back to the person who acts.
cards.lead: Today's grammar starts with a real scene. Read it once for the story and look only for the little words sich and mir. The next cards explain why they look different.

examples.de: Frau Weber ist auf der Treppe gestürzt.
examples.en: Frau Weber has fallen on the stairs.

examples.de: Sie hat sich wehgetan.
examples.en: She has hurt herself.

examples.de: Ich habe mir den Fuß verletzt.
examples.en: I have hurt my foot.

deeper.text: Notice the helper verbs: stürzen uses sein (ist gestürzt) because it describes a movement or a sudden change. Sich verletzen and sich wehtun use haben (hat sich verletzt). A good rule: if you must say where someone fell, think of sein. If you say what happened to the body, think of haben. You will see both in one sentence very often.

example.de: Ben ist gestürzt und hat sich wehgetan.
example.en: Ben has fallen and hurt himself.

cards.more: Imagine a short film script. First someone falls: that is only about Frau Weber. Then the doctor asks what happened to her body. Now the body is the topic. In German the body part gets its own place in the sentence, and the little word in front of it, sich or mir, says who the body belongs to. Do not try to understand all of it now. Only watch the two small words and notice that they are not always the same.
steps: Mira: Frau Weber ist auf der Treppe gestürzt!
Leon: Sie hat sich wehgetan. Ich rufe die 112 an.
Mira: Frau Weber, haben Sie sich verletzt?
Frau Weber: Ja, ich habe mir den Fuß verletzt. Er tut sehr weh.
Leon: Der Rettungswagen kommt gleich.

cards.title: Accusative again: Ich wasche mich
cards.body: A reflexive pronoun points back to the subject. Without another object the pronoun is accusative: ich mich, du dich, er sich, wir uns, ihr euch, sie sich. Ich wasche mich means: I wash myself.
cards.lead: You saw mich, mir and sich in the scene. First a quick look at the set you already know from A2: the pronoun for a person who does something to themselves and nothing else.

examples.de: Ich wasche mich.
examples.en: I wash myself.

examples.de: Er zieht sich an.
examples.en: He gets dressed.

examples.de: Wir beeilen uns.
examples.en: We hurry.

deeper.text: Sich is the same for er, sie, es, Sie and sie (plural). That includes polite Sie: Haben Sie sich wehgetan? In the plural uns and euch are the same in every case, too. So only two forms ever need your attention: mich/mir and dich/dir. The other four pronouns are safe.

example.de: Haben Sie sich wehgetan?
example.en: Have you hurt yourself?

cards.more: Picture a person in front of a mirror. Ich wasche mich: the washing goes from me back to me, and nothing else is in the sentence. That is the accusative reflexive. You know it from verbs like sich freuen, sich beeilen and sich anziehen. Nothing new here, only a short warm-up. Read the table once from top to bottom and say each example aloud. The next card shows what happens when something else enters the sentence, for example the hands.

cards.title: Extra object: Ich wasche mir die Hände
cards.body: If the sentence already has an accusative object (die Hände, die Zähne, das Bein), the pronoun cannot be accusative too. It becomes dative. Only ich and du change: mir and dir. Er, wir, ihr and sie keep sich, uns and euch.
cards.lead: Now the new step. What if the sentence says what you wash: the hands? This card shows the one change, and why the pronoun cannot stay accusative.

examples.de: Ich wasche mir die Hände.
examples.en: I wash my hands.

examples.de: Du wäschst dir das Gesicht.
examples.en: You wash your face.

examples.de: Mira kämmt sich die Haare.
examples.en: Mira combs her hair.

deeper.text: How do you know which case you need? Ask: is there already an object that I am doing something to? Die Hände is the object, so the pronoun is dative. In the er-form you cannot see the difference: Er wäscht sich and Er wäscht sich die Hände look the same. Only ich and du show it, so these are the forms to watch.

example.de: Er wäscht sich die Hände.
example.en: He washes his hands.

cards.more: Think of a seat with one place. Ich wasche mich: the pronoun sits in the accusative seat, because it is the only object. Ich wasche mir die Hände: now die Hände takes the accusative seat. The pronoun must move to the other seat, the dative seat, and mich becomes mir. It is just a seat change, not a new idea. And it only shows with ich and du, because sich, uns and euch look the same in both seats.

cards.title: Body and care: Zähne, Hände, Haare
cards.body: For care of your own body, German uses the pronoun, not mein. You say Ich putze mir die Zähne, not Ich putze meine Zähne. It is obvious whose teeth they are. Three verbs to learn: sich die Zähne putzen, sich die Hände waschen, sich die Haare kämmen.
cards.lead: With the rule from the last card you can talk about your daily care. This card gives three verbs that always carry a body part, so mir and dir appear again and again.

examples.de: Ich putze mir die Zähne.
examples.en: I brush my teeth.

examples.de: Du kämmst dir die Haare.
examples.en: You comb your hair.

examples.de: Leon wäscht sich die Hände.
examples.en: Leon washes his hands.

deeper.text: When you do this to another person, the pronoun is replaced by that person in the dative: Anna kämmt dem Kind die Haare. The body part stays the accusative object. So the dative stands for the owner of the body part, whether it is you (mir) or someone else (dem Kind). This is why the possessive mein is not needed.

example.de: Anna kämmt dem Kind die Haare.
example.en: Anna combs the child's hair.

cards.more: In English you say my teeth, my hands, my hair. German often does something different: it says the teeth to me, the hands to me. The little word mir tells you that the teeth belong to me. So the whole group works like a small machine: sich or mir, plus the body part with its article. Say the three phrases every morning in front of the mirror: Ich putze mir die Zähne. Ich wasche mir die Hände. Ich kämme mir die Haare.

cards.title: Accidents: sich den Knöchel brechen
cards.body: For accidents use sich (Dat) + body part + verb: sich den Knöchel brechen, sich den Fuß verletzen. In the Perfekt, haben stands in position 2, the pronoun comes right after it, the participle is last. Sich wehtun is a fixed chunk: Ich habe mir wehgetan.
cards.lead: Now the real story of the day. The same pattern describes accidents: you hurt a part of your body. The Perfekt with haben makes it a short report.

examples.de: Frau Weber hat sich den Knöchel gebrochen.
examples.en: Frau Weber has broken her ankle.

examples.de: Ich habe mir das Knie verletzt.
examples.en: I have hurt my knee.

examples.de: Leon hat sich wehgetan.
examples.en: Leon has hurt himself.

deeper.text: Do not mix up two things. Ich habe mir wehgetan tells what happened: an accident, a moment. Mein Bein tut weh describes a state: it hurts now. Wehtun always takes the person in the dative, like helfen, so mir stays even without a body part. A good pair: Ich habe mir wehgetan, und jetzt tut der Arm weh.

example.de: Mir tut das Bein weh.
example.en: My leg hurts.

cards.more: Tell an accident like a tiny news report with four boxes. Box one: who, with haben, in position 2. Box two: the little word sich or mir. Box three: the body part with its article. Box four: the participle at the very end. Frau Weber, hat, sich, den Knöchel, gebrochen. If you can fill the four boxes, you can report any small accident, and the doctor will understand you immediately.
steps: Subject + haben: Frau Weber hat
Pronoun right after haben: sich
Body part with article: den Knöchel
Participle at the end: gebrochen.

cards.title: The words: Knöchel, Gips, Krücken, Notaufnahme
cards.body: Learn each noun with its article and plural. The accident story uses six body words and five hospital words. Many of them end in -el, -en or -er and have the same plural as the singular: der Finger, die Finger.
cards.lead: You have the pattern, now you need the words that go with it. This card lists the body words and hospital words of the story with their articles and plurals.

examples.de: Der Rettungswagen fährt zur Notaufnahme.
examples.en: The ambulance drives to the emergency room.

examples.de: Frau Weber braucht einen Gips und Krücken.
examples.en: Frau Weber needs a plaster cast and crutches.

examples.de: Die Ärztin macht ein Röntgenbild.
examples.en: The doctor takes an X-ray.

deeper.text: In Germany the number 112 calls the Rettungswagen. It is free and works at any time. The Notaufnahme is for real emergencies, not for a small cold. Outside normal practice hours, the ärztlicher Bereitschaftsdienst answers under 116 117 in Germany. Many people do not know the difference, but it saves waiting time.

example.de: Bei einem Unfall ruft man die 112 an.
example.en: After an accident you call 112.

cards.more: Walk through a hospital in your head. First the Rettungswagen brings you in. You go to the Notaufnahme. The doctor makes a Röntgenbild and sees the Knochen. The ankle gets a Gips, and you walk away on Krücken. Make a picture for each word and put the picture in a place along that walk. Words with a picture and a place in a story stay in memory much longer than words from a list. Say the article each time.

cards.title: Put it together: in der Notaufnahme
cards.body: In the Notaufnahme the doctor asks questions with sich, and Frau Weber answers with mir. Read the dialogue in the steps. Then answer aloud: Haben Sie sich wehgetan? Ich habe mir den Knöchel verletzt.
cards.lead: This is the last card of the lesson. Use everything: a question with sich, an answer with mir, the Perfekt, and the new words. Read the dialogue and notice every little pronoun.

examples.de: Haben Sie sich wehgetan?
examples.en: Have you hurt yourself?

examples.de: Ich habe mir den Knöchel verletzt.
examples.en: I have hurt my ankle.

examples.de: Er tut sehr weh.
examples.en: It hurts a lot.

deeper.text: Notice that the doctor says Sie, so the answer uses ich: Haben Sie sich … Ich habe mir …. The pronoun follows the subject of each sentence, not the person you speak to. The doctor's sich belongs to Sie, Frau Weber's mir belongs to ich. A very common mistake is to answer with sich, copying the question.

example.de: Hat Leon sich den Finger verletzt?
example.en: Has Leon hurt his finger?

cards.more: Think of a ping-pong game. The doctor serves a question with sich, because the doctor talks about you. Frau Weber hits it back with mir, because she talks about herself. Every time the ball goes over the net, the pronoun changes with the speaker. Say the dialogue aloud with two voices and listen for sich, mir, sich, mir. Soon the right pronoun will come out by itself, without thinking about the rule.
steps: Ärztin: Was ist passiert, Frau Weber?
Frau Weber: Ich bin auf der Treppe gestürzt.
Ärztin: Haben Sie sich wehgetan?
Frau Weber: Ja, ich habe mir den Knöchel verletzt. Er tut sehr weh.
Ärztin: Wir machen ein Röntgenbild. Dann bekommt der Knöchel einen Gips.
Mira: Ich bleibe bei Ihnen, Frau Weber.

drills.explanation: Without another object the pronoun is accusative: Ich fühle mich nicht gut.

drills.prompt: Put in order: Frau Weber has broken her ankle.
drills.hint: haben in position 2, the pronoun right after it, the participle last.
drills.explanation: Frau Weber hat sich den Knöchel gebrochen.

drills.hint: er-form: does the pronoun change between the cases?

blind.prompt: Write in German: I have hurt my finger.

blind.hint: ich + haben, the pronoun right after it, the body part with article, participle last.
blind.explanation: Ich habe mir den Finger verletzt.

check.hint: wir: does the form depend on the case?
check.explanation: Wir waschen uns die Hände.

check.prompt: Ich habe ___ den Fuß verletzt. (Reflexivpronomen)
check.hint: den Fuß is already the accusative object.
check.explanation: Ich habe mir den Fuß verletzt.

check.prompt: Ich habe ___ gestern wehgetan. (Reflexivpronomen)

prompts: Say what you do every morning to your body: teeth, hands, hair. Use mir or dir.
Tell about a small accident: what you have hurt and what you needed.
Pretend you are Frau Weber in the Notaufnahme and answer the doctor's question: Haben Sie sich wehgetan?
examples: Jeden Morgen putze ich mir die Zähne und wasche mir das Gesicht. Dann kämme ich mir die Haare.
Ich bin gestern gestürzt und habe mir das Knie verletzt. Ich brauche ein Pflaster.
Ja, ich habe mir den Knöchel verletzt. Er tut sehr weh.

lessons.title: Besuchszeit: offering help, and the info sheet
lessons.goal: Read a hospital info sheet and find what you need, follow the rules with Sie commands, and offer help and answer politely.

grammar.topic: Offering help and hospital rules (use of lesson 1, no new rule)
grammar.point: Offer help with Soll ich …?, Kann ich … helfen?, Ich könnte … or Darf ich …?. Helfen takes the dative: Kann ich Ihnen helfen? Hospital rules use Sie commands with the reflexive pronoun and a body part: Desinfizieren Sie sich bitte die Hände.

mistake.why: Helfen takes the dative, so the person is Ihnen (or dir), never Sie or dich.

terms.meaning: the fixed hours when visitors may come to a ward
a question that offers to do something for someone: Soll ich …? Kann ich …?
a masculine noun that adds -en in every case except the nominative: der Patient, den Patienten

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Wo tut es weh?' to 'Besuchszeit'
cards.body: On Sunday Mira and Leon visit Frau Weber on the ward. At the door they need to read a short info sheet and understand the rules. Then they want to be useful: offer help and hear a polite answer. Today is about the real language of a hospital visit.
steps: You already know: Nehmen Sie die Tablette. At the doctor you heard commands with Sie in A1 chapter 8.
New today: Desinfizieren Sie sich bitte die Hände. Kann ich Ihnen helfen? The commands now carry the reflexive pronoun from lesson 1, and you can offer help.
By the end you can: read an info sheet, follow hospital rules and offer help politely.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie die Tablette.
examples.en: Take the tablet.
examples.why: You know this: a command with Sie.

examples.de: Desinfizieren Sie sich bitte die Hände.
examples.en: Please disinfect your hands.
examples.why: New today: the same command with sich and a body part, as in lesson 1.

cards.more: This lesson has no new rule. Think of it as a day out with tools you already own. From lesson 1 you take sich and the body part. From A1 you take the Sie command and helfen with the dative. Add a few polite sentences for offering help, and you can walk into a hospital, read the sheet at the door and talk to the nurse. Real German is often a mix of small pieces that you already know, put together for a real place.

cards.title: At the Station: Anmeldung and Besuchszeit
cards.body: A hospital visit starts at the desk of the Station (ward). The nurse tells you the room and the Besuchszeit. A Einzelzimmer is for one patient, a Doppelzimmer for two. The Gesundheitskarte is the card that the patient shows at admission.
cards.lead: First the scene at the ward desk. Listen for the words you need on every visit: room, visiting hours and the health insurance card.

examples.de: Wir möchten Frau Weber besuchen.
examples.en: We would like to visit Frau Weber.

examples.de: Sie liegt in einem Einzelzimmer.
examples.en: She is in a single room.

examples.de: Die Besuchszeit ist am Nachmittag.
examples.en: Visiting time is in the afternoon.

deeper.text: Notice the prepositions: Frau Weber liegt auf der Station (on the ward), but in der Notaufnahme and im Zimmer. For a ward, German thinks of a level or an area, so it uses auf. Station is feminine: die Station. Visiting hours are usually in the afternoon and early evening, and they are fixed.

example.de: Frau Weber liegt auf der Station.
example.en: Frau Weber is on the ward.

cards.more: Imagine you arrive at a hotel. You go to the desk, say who you want to see, and get the room and the times. A hospital is very similar. The nurse is like the receptionist. The Station is the floor, the Zimmer is the room, and the Besuchszeit is the time when guests may come. You just need the words for the desk. Read the dialogue in the steps aloud, once as Mira and once as the nurse.
steps: Mira: Guten Tag, wir möchten Frau Weber besuchen.
Krankenschwester: Sie liegt in einem Einzelzimmer. Hier ist Ihr Besucherausweis.
Leon: Ist jetzt Besuchszeit?
Krankenschwester: Ja, die Besuchszeit ist am Nachmittag und am frühen Abend.
Mira: Hat Frau Weber ihre Gesundheitskarte dabei?
Krankenschwester: Ja, sie hat die Karte gestern bei der Aufnahme gezeigt. Die Tür ist links.

cards.title: The info sheet: read the headings first
cards.body: Info sheets have headings: Besuchszeiten, Handy, Hygiene, Ruhe. Strategy: 1. Read only the headings. 2. Find the times and the rules you need. 3. Skip the rest. Read the sheet in the steps and find when you may visit.
cards.lead: At the door hangs a short sheet. You do not need to understand every word. This card gives a three-step strategy for reading texts like this one.

examples.de: Bitte Handy leise stellen.
examples.en: Please set your phone to silent.

examples.de: Am Abend ist Nachtruhe.
examples.en: In the evening there is night quiet.

examples.de: Bitte desinfizieren Sie sich die Hände.
examples.en: Please disinfect your hands.

deeper.text: Info sheets and signs often use the infinitive or bitte plus the Sie form for rules: Bitte Handy ausschalten. Bitte leise sprechen. There is no subject and no Sie, it is just short. In your own speech you would say Schalten Sie bitte das Handy aus. Both forms mean the same, but the sign style is only written.

example.de: Bitte leise sprechen.
example.en: Please speak quietly.

cards.more: When you look at a menu in a restaurant, you do not read every word. You look at the headings: starters, main dishes, drinks. Then you look for the thing you want. An info sheet works the same way. Four headings, four little blocks. If you want to know when to come, you only open the block with Besuchszeiten. This saves energy, and you stay calm even when the text has words that you do not know yet.
steps: Besuchszeiten: täglich am Nachmittag und am frühen Abend
Handy: Bitte leise stellen oder nur kurz telefonieren.
Hygiene: Bitte desinfizieren Sie sich die Hände.
Ruhe: Am Abend ist Nachtruhe. Bitte sprechen Sie leise.

cards.title: Hospital rules: what visitors do
cards.body: Rules are often commands with Sie or sentences with dürfen. Visitors disinfect their hands, switch the phone to silent or keep calls short, and are quiet in the rooms. The word bitte makes a command friendly. The reflexive pronoun is sich with Sie.
cards.lead: Now the rules in detail. You have seen them on the sheet. This card shows which sentences you hear and say as a visitor.

examples.de: Sie dürfen Frau Weber am Nachmittag besuchen.
examples.en: You may visit Frau Weber in the afternoon.

examples.de: Desinfizieren Sie sich bitte die Hände.
examples.en: Please disinfect your hands.

examples.de: Bitte sprechen Sie leise.
examples.en: Please speak quietly.

deeper.text: The rules are a tendency and differ between hospitals. The visiting times hang at the entrance and on the ward, so read them there. Some wards have shorter times, some allow more guests. When you are unsure, ask the nurse: Darf ich noch bleiben? That question is polite and shows that you respect the ward.

example.de: Die Besuchszeiten hängen am Eingang.
example.en: The visiting times hang at the entrance.

cards.more: Think of a hospital as a house with house rules, like in your WG. The rules protect the patients, who are tired and need quiet and clean hands. Many people in Germany expect visitors to follow them without being told. So you learn four short sentences by heart: hands, phone, quiet, time. With these four you are a good guest on any ward, and nobody has to remind you.

cards.title: Hospital words: Patient, Pfleger, Visite
cards.body: Learn the people and routines with article and plural: die Krankenschwester, der Pfleger, der Patient, die Visite, die Untersuchung, die Entlassung, der Rollstuhl. Der Patient is special: it adds -en in every case except the nominative.
cards.lead: Rules mention people and routines. This card collects the words for who works on the ward and what happens there, with articles and plurals.

examples.de: Der Pfleger hilft dem Patienten.

examples.de: Die Visite ist am Vormittag.
examples.en: The ward round is in the morning.

examples.de: Frau Weber sitzt im Rollstuhl.

deeper.text: Der Patient belongs to the n-declension, which you know from B1 chapter 1: den Patienten, dem Patienten. Der Pfleger is not an n-noun: der Pfleger, dem Pfleger. Both end in -er or -ent, so look at each word separately. Because you often talk about patients in hospital stories, this is a useful detail to remember.

example.de: Die Ärztin spricht mit dem Patienten.
example.en: The doctor speaks with the patient.

cards.more: Picture the ward as a small team. The Krankenschwester and the Pfleger look after the patients every day. Once a day the doctors come for the Visite and look at every patient. Sometimes there is an Untersuchung, a check. And after some days the patient hears the best word: Entlassung, going home. Put each word on this little time line and say the article. Remember: der Patient, den Patienten, dem Patienten.

rows: der Patient, die Patienten (den, dem Patienten)

cards.title: Offering help: Soll ich …? Kann ich Ihnen helfen?
cards.body: To offer help, use Soll ich …?, Kann ich … helfen?, Ich könnte … or Darf ich …?. Helfen takes the dative: Kann ich Ihnen helfen? The infinitive stands at the end, as with every modal verb.
cards.lead: Mira and Leon want to do something for Frau Weber. This card gives four ways to offer help, from direct to very polite, and shows the dative with helfen.

examples.de: Soll ich Ihnen die Post bringen?
examples.en: Shall I bring you the post?

examples.de: Kann ich Ihnen helfen?
examples.en: Can I help you?

examples.de: Ich könnte morgen nach der Katze sehen.
examples.en: I could look after the cat tomorrow.

deeper.text: The four forms are a little different. Soll ich …? offers to do something: it asks for a wish. Kann ich …? asks if something is possible or allowed. Ich könnte … is a soft suggestion. Darf ich …? is the most polite form. With people you do not know well, Darf ich Ihnen helfen? is a good choice.

example.de: Darf ich Ihnen die Tasche tragen?
example.en: May I carry your bag for you?

cards.more: Offering help is like holding out a hand. You can say it in a direct way, Soll ich …?, or in a careful way, Darf ich …?. Because helfen belongs to the dative group, the person you help is Ihnen or dir, never Sie or dich. Remember it as one pair: Ich helfe Ihnen. The thing you do goes to the end of the sentence. Then you can offer everything: the post, the bag, the cat.

rows: Soll ich Ihnen die Post bringen?

cards.title: Saying yes and no politely
cards.body: To accept: Ja, gern. / Das wäre nett. / Danke, das ist sehr freundlich. To decline: Nein danke, das schaffe ich allein. / Das ist nicht nötig. A bare Nein sounds blunt: always add danke and a short reason.
cards.lead: A good offer needs a good answer. This card gives you the sentences for accepting and for declining in a friendly way.

examples.de: Das wäre nett, danke.
examples.en: That would be nice, thanks.

examples.de: Danke, das ist sehr freundlich.
examples.en: Thanks, that is very kind.

examples.de: Das schaffe ich allein.
examples.en: I can manage that alone.

deeper.text: Das wäre nett uses the Konjunktiv II of sein, which you know from B1 chapter 5. It makes the answer softer than Das ist nett. And a short sentence of thanks is common even when you say no: Nein, danke, das ist nicht nötig. Later you will meet a useful chunk for this: Das brauchen Sie nicht.

example.de: Nein, danke, das ist nicht nötig.
example.en: No, thanks, that is not necessary.

cards.more: Imagine two doors. Behind the first door is yes: you smile and say gern or das wäre nett. Behind the second door is no: you smile, say danke and give a small reason, for example I can do it alone. In both cases there is a little word of thanks. This is the key for politeness in German: no answer is naked, it always wears a small thank you. Practise both doors with the same offer: Soll ich die Post bringen?

rows: Nein danke, das schaffe ich allein.
Danke, das ist nett, aber es geht schon.

cards.title: Put it together: a visit on the Station
cards.body: At the Station Mira, Leon, the nurse and Frau Weber talk. Read the dialogue in the steps. Find three things: a rule, an offer and an answer. Then say the lines aloud with a partner or alone with two voices.
cards.lead: The last card uses everything: the desk words, the rules, an offer and a polite answer. Read the dialogue and notice every offer and every answer.

examples.en: That would be very nice.

deeper.text: Notice Sie haben Besuch. The word Besuch means both the visit and the visitors, and it has no plural. You say Frau Weber hat Besuch, not Besuche. In German you also say Besuch bekommen (to get visitors). This is a small phrase that you will hear very often on a ward.

example.de: Frau Weber hat heute viel Besuch.
example.en: Frau Weber has a lot of visitors today.

cards.more: This is the whole visit in one scene. The nurse welcomes the guests and reminds them about the hands. Mira asks how she can help. Leon offers to bring the post. Frau Weber answers with das wäre sehr nett. You could play every one of these roles in real life. If you can say these lines without looking, you are ready for your first real visit in a German hospital.

lessons.title: Was wünschst du dir? More verbs with mir/dir
lessons.goal: Use the many everyday verbs with a dative reflexive pronoun, also separable ones in the Perfekt, and say what you wish for, look at, listen to and treat yourself to.

grammar.topic: Dative reflexive verbs: sich (Dat) etwas wünschen, ansehen, anhören, gönnen …
grammar.point: The rule from lesson 1 applies to many verbs: when the sentence has an accusative object, ich and du use mir and dir (Ich wünsche mir ein Hörbuch). With separable verbs the prefix goes to the end: Ich sehe mir den Film an; Perfekt: Ich habe mir den Film angesehen. The pronoun stands right after the verb or after a pronoun subject.
grammar.oneLine: Ich sehe mir den Film an.

mistake.wrong: Ich sehe mich den Film an.
mistake.right: Ich sehe mir den Film an.
mistake.why: The film is the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun is dative: mir. The prefix an stays at the end.

terms.meaning: a verb whose prefix goes to the end of the main clause: ansehen, anhören, aufschreiben
a verb that uses mir or dir with an accusative object: sich etwas wünschen
the usual meaning of mir or dir in this group of verbs

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich wasche mir die Hände' to 'Ich sehe mir einen Film an'
cards.body: Mira and Leon ask Frau Weber what they should bring to the hospital. She answers with a very German pattern: Ich wünsche mir ein Hörbuch. The little word mir comes back, but now there is no body part. Today you learn the big group of everyday verbs that use it.
steps: You already know: Ich wasche mir die Hände. With an extra object, ich becomes mir and du becomes dir (lesson 1).
New today: Ich höre mir ein Hörbuch an. Ich wünsche mir Blumen. The rule is the same, but the object can be anything you want, buy, look at or listen to.
By the end you can: say what you wish for, look at, listen to and treat yourself to.

examples.de: Ich wasche mir die Hände.
examples.en: I wash my hands.
examples.why: You know this: mir with an object.

examples.de: Ich höre mir ein Hörbuch an.
examples.en: I listen to an audiobook.
examples.why: New today: the same mir, with a thing instead of a body part, and a separable verb.

cards.more: Lesson 1 gave you one rule: when a sentence already has an accusative object, ich and du use mir and dir. That rule does not care what the object is. It can be your teeth, but it can also be an audiobook, a coffee or a break. Many everyday German verbs simply come with this little extra word. It often means for myself or to myself. So today is not a new rule. It is a list of useful verbs that follow the old one.

cards.title: What to bring Frau Weber
cards.body: Mira and Leon visit Frau Weber and ask what she wants. She answers with wishes. Read the dialogue in the steps and look for mir and sich. They stand next to things she wants: a Hörbuch, a Kreuzworträtsel, Hausschuhe, Pralinen.
cards.lead: First the scene in the hospital room. Listen to Frau Weber and look for the little word mir and its friends, in a place where there is no body part at all.

examples.de: Ich wünsche mir ein Hörbuch.
examples.en: I wish for an audiobook.

examples.de: Wir bringen Ihnen Blumen mit.
examples.en: We bring you flowers.

examples.de: Die gönne ich mir heute.
examples.en: I treat myself to those today.

deeper.text: Compare two sentences. Wir bringen Ihnen Blumen mit: the flowers are for another person, so you use Ihnen. Ich bringe mir Blumen mit: the flowers are for me, so you use mir. The same position, the same case, only the person changes. A reflexive pronoun is just the dative of the person who is also the subject.

example.de: Ich bringe mir Blumen mit.
example.en: I bring myself flowers.

cards.more: Imagine a gift shop. When you buy a present for a friend, you say: Ich kaufe dir ein Buch. When you buy it for yourself, you say: Ich kaufe mir ein Buch. The only difference is who gets the gift. The little word mir tells you that you are the one who gets it. So the pronoun is not mysterious at all: it is the receiver of the thing. Keep this picture in your head when you read the dialogue.
steps: Mira: Frau Weber, was sollen wir Ihnen mitbringen?
Frau Weber: Ich wünsche mir ein Hörbuch. Am Abend höre ich mir gern eine Geschichte an.
Leon: Ich bringe Ihnen auch ein Kreuzworträtsel mit.
Frau Weber: Gern. Und meine Hausschuhe, bitte.
Mira: Wir kaufen noch einen Blumenstrauß.
Frau Weber: Das ist lieb. Und vielleicht Pralinen? Die gönne ich mir heute.

cards.title: The rule again: no body part, the same pronoun
cards.body: With these verbs the pronoun is dative because there is already an accusative object: sich etwas wünschen, ansehen, anhören, holen, kaufen. It often means for myself. Only ich and du change: mir and dir. Sich, uns and euch stay.
cards.lead: Lesson 1 used body parts. Here is the same rule with other objects. This card shows five everyday verbs where the thing you want, get or look at is the accusative object.

examples.de: Ich kaufe mir Pralinen.
examples.en: I buy myself chocolates.

examples.de: Er holt sich einen Kaffee.
examples.en: He gets himself a coffee.

examples.de: Du wünschst dir einen Blumenstrauß.
examples.en: You wish for a bouquet.

deeper.text: Careful with sich vorstellen: it has two meanings. With the accusative it means to introduce yourself: Ich stelle mich vor. With the dative and an object it means to imagine: Ich stelle mir das vor. The little word shows which one: mich is only one object, mir comes with a second object like das or ein Zimmer.

example.de: Ich stelle mir ein ruhiges Zimmer vor.
example.en: I imagine a quiet room.

cards.more: Think of the pronoun as a small label on the thing: for me. Ich kaufe mir Pralinen means I buy chocolates for me. Er holt sich einen Kaffee means he gets a coffee for himself. This is not just grammar, it is also meaning: the verb with mir often says that you do it for yourself or for your own pleasure. If you are unsure which pronoun to use, ask yourself: what is the object? If there is one, take mir or dir.

rows: Du siehst dir den Film an.
Wir hören uns die Musik an.

cards.title: Separable verbs: Ich sehe mir den Film an
cards.body: With a separable verb the prefix goes to the end: Ich sehe mir den Film an. The pronoun stays right after the verb. In the Perfekt, haben is in position 2 and the participle is last: Ich habe mir den Film angesehen.
cards.lead: Several of these verbs are separable: ansehen, anhören, aufschreiben. This card shows where mir stands and what happens to the prefix.

examples.de: Ich sehe mir den Film an.
examples.en: I watch the film.

examples.de: Frau Weber hört sich ein Hörbuch an.
examples.en: Frau Weber listens to an audiobook.

examples.de: Ich habe mir den Film angesehen.
examples.en: I have watched the film.

deeper.text: When the object is a pronoun (es, ihn, sie), the order changes: the accusative pronoun comes first and the dative pronoun second. You say Ich sehe ihn mir an, not Ich sehe mir ihn an. With a noun the dative pronoun comes first: Ich sehe mir den Film an. This is a rule of word order in German.

example.de: Ich sehe ihn mir an.
example.en: I look at it (the film).

cards.more: Picture a drawer with a zip. In the present, the verb sehe stands up front and its prefix an waits at the very end, like the end of the zip. In between there is room for mir and the object: sehe, mir, den Film, an. In the Perfekt the two parts of the verb come together again: angesehen, with ge in the middle. The pronoun mir is not affected by any of this. It always stays right behind the verb.
steps: Verb in position 2: Ich sehe
Pronoun right after it: mir
The thing you look at: den Film
The prefix at the very end: an.

cards.title: Treating yourself: gönnen, leisten, holen
cards.body: Sich etwas gönnen means to treat yourself: Ich gönne mir eine Pause. Sich etwas leisten means to be able to afford it: Ich kann mir das leisten. Sich etwas holen means to go and get something for yourself: Ich hole mir einen Tee.
cards.lead: The next group says something nice: you do something good for yourself. This card gives you sentences for a break, a treat and for what you can afford.

examples.de: Ich gönne mir eine Pause.
examples.en: I treat myself to a break.

examples.de: Frau Weber gönnt sich Pralinen.
examples.en: Frau Weber treats herself to chocolates.

examples.de: Das kann ich mir leisten.
examples.en: I can afford that.

deeper.text: Gönnen also works with another person: Ich gönne dir den Urlaub means I am happy that you get this holiday, I do not envy you. Now the person is in the dative and the thing in the accusative. So the pattern gönnen + dative + accusative is the same, whether the person is you or someone else. Related: verwöhnen means to spoil someone with something nice.

example.de: Ich gönne dir den Urlaub.
example.en: I am happy that you get the holiday.

cards.more: Think about a lazy Sunday. You make a cup of tea, you take a break, maybe you buy a small cake. In German each of these little treats comes with mir: Ich hole mir einen Tee, ich gönne mir eine Pause, ich kaufe mir einen Kuchen. When you are in the hospital like Frau Weber, you need these little moments even more. Learn the phrase Ich gönne mir eine Auszeit. It is perfect for a week with a broken ankle.

rows: to be able to afford something

cards.title: Memory and notes: merken, aufschreiben, überlegen
cards.body: Sich etwas merken means to remember it: Ich merke mir die Nummer. Sich etwas aufschreiben means to note it down: Ich schreibe mir das auf. Sich etwas überlegen means to think it over: Das überlege ich mir. Stell dir vor! means Imagine!
cards.lead: Some of these verbs are about your head and not about things: remembering, writing down, thinking over. This card shows three verbs that you can use every day at school or at work.

examples.de: Ich merke mir die Nummer.
examples.en: I remember the number.

examples.de: Mira schreibt sich den Termin auf.
examples.en: Mira writes down the appointment.

examples.de: Stell dir vor!
examples.en: Imagine!

deeper.text: Überlegen exists with and without mir. Ich überlege means I am thinking. Ich überlege mir das means I am thinking it over to decide, the answer will come later. It is a very common polite way to say not yet: Das überlege ich mir noch. It shows that you take the question seriously and do not say no.

example.de: Das überlege ich mir noch.
example.en: I will think it over.

cards.more: Think of a small notebook that every person has in their head. Sich etwas merken means: I put the thing in my own notebook. Sich etwas aufschreiben means: I write it in a real notebook. And sich etwas überlegen means: I take the thing out and look at it for a while. In all three the thing is the object, and mir says that it is my own notebook. This helps you to remember the whole group: mir means for my own head and my own use.

cards.title: Word order: where does mir stand?
cards.body: In a main clause the pronoun stands right after the verb, or after a pronoun subject: Heute gönne ich mir eine Pause. After a noun subject it stands before the noun: Heute gönnt sich Frau Weber eine Pause. In a weil- or dass-clause it stands right after the subject.
cards.lead: You know the pronoun comes after the verb. This card shows the three typical places: after the verb, after a pronoun subject and inside a weil-clause.

examples.de: Heute gönne ich mir eine Pause.
examples.en: Today I treat myself to a break.

examples.de: Heute gönnt sich Frau Weber ein Hörbuch.
examples.en: Today Frau Weber treats herself to an audiobook.

examples.de: Ich bleibe hier, weil ich mir Zeit nehme.
examples.en: I stay here because I take my time.

deeper.text: In speech people often shorten the verb: Ich hab mir ein Buch geholt. The hab is the spoken form of habe, and you will hear it a lot, but you write habe. The word order does not change: hab, mir, the object, the participle. If you can say it in the long form, the short form is easy.

example.de: Ich hab mir ein Buch geholt.
example.en: I got myself a book.

cards.more: Think of the reflexive pronoun as a shadow of the subject. It likes to stand close. With a short pronoun subject like ich or sie, the shadow is right behind it: gönne ich mir. With a noun like Frau Weber the shadow goes in front: gönnt sich Frau Weber. In a weil-clause the shadow follows the subject again: weil ich mir. If you remember the shadow, you will find the right place nearly every time.

Heute gönnt sich Frau Weber eine Pause.

cards.title: Gute Besserung! Wishes
cards.body: To wish something to another person use the dative: Ich wünsche dir gute Besserung! To wish something for yourself, use mir: Ich wünsche mir ein Hörbuch. After wünschen you can also use a dass-clause: Ich wünsche mir, dass du bald kommst.
cards.lead: The last card brings the lesson back to the hospital. It shows how to wish something to another person and to yourself, and the fixed phrase for sick people.

examples.en: I wish you a speedy recovery.

examples.de: Ich wünsche mir, dass du bald kommst.

examples.de: Gute Besserung!
examples.en: Get well soon!

deeper.text: Gute Besserung is only for sick or hurt people. For other occasions you say Alles Gute, for example before an exam or for a birthday. A warmer, informal wish to a friend is Werde bald wieder gesund! You can also write it on a card. The word Besserung means improvement, and gute is the adjective without an article, just as in Gute Nacht.

example.de: Werde bald wieder gesund!
example.en: Get well again soon!

cards.more: Wishes follow the same two roads as everything in this lesson. If the wish is for another person, you put that person in the dative: dir, Ihnen. If the wish is for you, you use mir. A wish for yourself can also be a whole idea: Ich wünsche mir, dass du bald kommst. The sentence after dass sends the verb to the end, as you know from earlier chapters. And when a friend is ill, you do not need to think: Gute Besserung! always fits.
steps: Wish for another person: Ich wünsche dir gute Besserung!
Wish for yourself: Ich wünsche mir ein Hörbuch.
Wish with dass: Ich wünsche mir, dass du bald kommst.
To an ill friend: Gute Besserung!

lessons.title: Ihr braucht nicht jeden Tag zu kommen: brauchen + zu
lessons.goal: Say that something is not necessary with nicht, kein or nur + brauchen + zu + infinitive, also with separable and reflexive verbs.

grammar.point: Brauchen + nicht/kein/nur + zu + infinitive means 'no need' (nicht, kein) or 'only need' (nur). Zu stands in front of the infinitive and inside separable verbs (anzurufen). A reflexive pronoun stays before zu. In a side clause the order is zu + infinitive + brauchen. Without nicht, kein or nur, use müssen.

mistake.why: Brauchen is not a modal verb, so the second verb needs zu. People drop zu in speech, but written German needs it.

terms.meaning: brauchen with an infinitive and zu; used with nicht, kein or nur: no need or only need
a clause that cannot stand alone; the finite verb is at the end: …, dass du nicht zu kommen brauchst.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Du musst nicht kommen' to 'Du brauchst nicht zu kommen'
cards.body: Frau Weber is home with a cast and crutches. The WG wants to help every day, but she says: Ihr braucht nicht jeden Tag zu kommen. Today you learn the polite, written way to say that something is not necessary: nicht, kein or nur with brauchen + zu.
steps: You already know: Du musst nicht kommen. (you do not have to come)
New today: Du brauchst nicht zu kommen. And: Du brauchst nur anzurufen. (you only have to call)
By the end you can: say what is not necessary with nicht, kein and nur, also with separable and reflexive verbs.

examples.de: Du musst nicht kommen.
examples.en: You do not have to come.
examples.why: You know this: müssen with nicht.

examples.de: Du brauchst nicht zu kommen.
examples.en: You do not need to come.
examples.why: New today: brauchen + nicht + zu + infinitive.

examples.de: Du brauchst nur anzurufen.
examples.en: You only need to call.
examples.why: New today: nur, and zu inside anzurufen.

examples.de: Ihr braucht keinen Termin zu machen.
examples.en: You do not need to make an appointment.
examples.why: New today: kein + noun.

cards.more: Think of the word brauchen as a small door sign that says: not necessary. In normal speech you say müssen with nicht. In careful or written German you swap müssen for brauchen, and because brauchen is not a real modal verb, it asks for the little word zu before the second verb. Same meaning, slightly more polite and more written. You will hear it from teachers, in letters and in notices, so it is worth learning cleanly.

cards.title: Frau Weber is home
cards.body: Frau Weber sits in her armchair with a cast. Mira and Leon bring soup and want to come every day. She smiles and refuses politely. Look at the verb brauchen and the little word zu: they stand together, with the second verb at the very end of the clause.
cards.lead: This first card is only a scene. Read the short dialogue and spot the two parts that belong together: a form of brauchen in second place and zu right in front of the verb at the end.

examples.de: Ihr braucht nicht jeden Tag zu kommen.
examples.en: You do not need to come every day.

examples.de: Sie brauchen sich keine Sorgen zu machen, Frau Weber.
examples.en: You do not need to worry, Frau Weber.

examples.de: Ich brauche heute nicht zu kochen.
examples.en: I do not need to cook today.

deeper.text: Frau Weber says ihr to the whole WG, and the four say Sie to her. That is why the same idea appears as Ihr braucht and as Sie brauchen in one dialogue. The pattern itself never changes: a form of brauchen, then nicht or kein, then zu, then the infinitive at the end.

example.de: Wir brauchen nicht zu warten.
example.en: We do not need to wait.

cards.more: Imagine a seesaw. On the left sits brauchen, close to the start of the sentence. On the right, far away at the end, sits the infinitive. In the middle you put what belongs to the sentence: who, when, what. The little word zu sits right on the right end, just before the infinitive, like a handle on a door. When you see brauchen in a negative sentence and an infinitive far away at the end, always look for that handle zu before it.
steps: Mira: Wir kommen morgen wieder.
Frau Weber: Ihr braucht nicht jeden Tag zu kommen.
Leon: Aber wir machen uns Sorgen.
Frau Weber: Ihr braucht euch keine Sorgen zu machen.

cards.title: nicht müssen = nicht brauchen zu
cards.body: Nicht brauchen + zu means the same as nicht müssen: there is no need. Nicht stands after the subject and the verb, zu stands directly before the infinitive, and the infinitive is last. Everything else, like a time word or an object, goes in between.
cards.lead: You saw brauchen with zu in the scene. Now you compare it with the verb you already know, müssen, and learn where nicht and zu sit in the clause.

examples.de: Du musst nicht warten.
examples.en: You do not have to wait.

examples.de: Du brauchst nicht zu warten.
examples.en: You do not need to wait.

examples.de: Mira braucht heute nicht zu arbeiten.
examples.en: Mira does not need to work today.

deeper.text: Careful: nicht brauchen zu is NOT the same as nicht dürfen. Du brauchst nicht zu gehen means you may stay, there is no need to leave. Du darfst nicht gehen means it is forbidden. Müssen and brauchen negate to 'no need'; dürfen negates to 'forbidden'.

example.de: Du darfst nicht gehen.
example.en: You must not go (forbidden).

cards.more: Picture a traffic light with three colours. Müssen is red: you have to. Dürfen is green: you may. When you add nicht, the lights change differently. Nicht müssen turns into a free choice: you can, but you do not have to. Brauchen + nicht + zu says exactly that, only with a more written feel. Nicht dürfen, however, is a wall: it is not allowed. If you only keep one thing, keep this: no need is brauchen, no permission is dürfen.

cards.title: kein + noun
cards.body: When the verb has an object without an article, or with ein, you negate it with kein, not with nicht. Kein stands in front of the noun and takes the usual endings. The rest stays the same: brauchen, the object, then zu and the infinitive at the end.
cards.lead: So far nicht stood alone. Now the thing you do not need to do has a noun with it, for example a pill or an appointment, and German then prefers kein over nicht.

examples.de: Du brauchst keine Tabletten zu nehmen.
examples.en: You do not need to take any pills.

examples.de: Wir brauchen keinen Termin zu machen.
examples.en: We do not need to make an appointment.

examples.de: Ihr braucht kein Geschenk mitzubringen.
examples.en: You do not need to bring a present.

deeper.text: Kein is also a gentle way to reassure someone: Du brauchst keine Angst zu haben. (You do not need to be afraid.) Doctors, teachers and friends say this all the time. With a noun that has no article, such as Angst, Sorgen or Hilfe, German always uses kein plus brauchen + zu.

example.de: Du brauchst keine Angst zu haben.
example.en: You do not need to be afraid.

cards.more: Think of kein as nicht plus ein squeezed into one word. You do not say: you do not need to take pills with a nicht floating around. Instead you say: you need to take no pills, and the no belongs directly to the noun. Like ein, kein changes with the noun: keine Tabletten, keinen Termin, kein Geschenk. If there is a noun without an article, grab kein. If there is no noun, or the noun has der, die, das, use nicht.

rows: Du brauchst keine Tabletten zu nehmen.
Wir brauchen keinen Termin zu machen.

cards.title: nur: you only have to
cards.body: With nur, brauchen is positive in meaning: Du brauchst nur anzurufen means you only have to call, it is enough. This is the one case where brauchen + zu needs no nicht and no kein. Nur takes the place of nicht, just before the infinitive part.
cards.lead: After no need comes its mirror: just this one small thing is needed. You still use brauchen and zu, but nur replaces nicht and the sentence becomes positive.

examples.de: Ihr braucht nur anzurufen.
examples.en: You only need to call.

examples.de: Sie brauchen nur zu klingeln.
examples.en: You only need to ring the bell.

examples.de: Du brauchst nur zu sagen, was du brauchst.
examples.en: You only need to say what you need.

deeper.text: Nur zu klingeln is the same as Du musst nur klingeln: the meaning is a small effort. Herr Ali says it to a guest who is shy to ask: Sie brauchen nur zu fragen. It is a friendly sentence that tells someone: it costs you nothing, just ask.

example.de: Sie brauchen nur zu fragen.
example.en: You only need to ask.

cards.more: Imagine a short bridge. Without nur, brauchen needs a nicht or a kein. That is the rule most people learn, and it is a good safe one. Nur is the little exception that opens a second door: you only have to do this one thing. Because the meaning is not negative, nothing is taken away, you just say that very little is needed. When you hear nur next to brauchen, think of the word only: only call, only ask, only ring.

rows: Ihr braucht keinen Anruf zu machen.

cards.title: Separable and reflexive verbs
cards.body: With a separable verb, zu goes inside the verb, between the prefix and the stem: anzurufen, mitzubringen, aufzuräumen. With a reflexive verb, the reflexive pronoun stays in front of zu: Du brauchst dich nicht zu beeilen. Du brauchst dir keine Sorgen zu machen.
cards.lead: Many everyday verbs are separable or reflexive. This card shows where zu goes in the two cases and brings back the mir and dir from lesson 1.

examples.de: Du brauchst nicht anzurufen.
examples.en: You do not need to call.

examples.de: Du brauchst dich nicht zu beeilen.
examples.en: You do not need to hurry.

examples.de: Du brauchst dir keine Sorgen zu machen.
examples.en: You do not need to worry.

deeper.text: Both reflexive examples use the pronouns from lessons 1 to 3. Beeilen takes the accusative: dich. Sich Sorgen machen has an accusative object, Sorgen, so the pronoun is dative: dir. The pronoun always stands directly after brauchen or after the subject, never next to zu.

example.de: Du brauchst dir nichts zu verbieten.
example.en: You do not need to forbid yourself anything.

cards.more: Think of zu as a small word that likes to stand in front of the second verb. If the verb is a whole piece, like machen, zu stands in front of it. If the verb has a prefix that can fall off, like an in anrufen, zu slips in between and glues the verb back together: anzurufen. The reflexive pronoun is different, it is a passenger that sits next to brauchen. So the order is: brauchen, pronoun, nicht or kein, zu, infinitive.

rows: Du brauchst dich nicht zu beeilen.
Du brauchst dir keine Sorgen zu machen.

cards.title: In side clauses
cards.body: In a side clause with dass or wenn, the verb goes to the end. With brauchen + zu both verbs end up there: zu + infinitive first, then brauchen. So: Ich sage dir, dass du nicht zu kommen brauchst. You only need to recognise this order; in speech, you can avoid it.
cards.lead: So far brauchen stood in second place. Now the whole thing moves into a dass or wenn clause, and brauchen drops to the very end, behind the infinitive.

examples.de: Ich sage dir, dass du nicht zu kommen brauchst.
examples.en: I tell you that you do not need to come.

examples.de: Mira sagt, dass wir nicht zu warten brauchen.
examples.en: Mira says that we do not need to wait.

examples.de: Wenn du nur anzurufen brauchst, ruf mich an.
examples.en: If you only need to call, call me.

deeper.text: Many Germans avoid the long order and say two sentences instead: Du brauchst nicht zu kommen. Das sage ich dir. Both versions are correct. Reading the long version is a good test: when a clause ends in two verbs, the last one is the one that carries the person, in this case brauchst.

example.de: Du brauchst nicht zu kommen.
example.en: You do not need to come.

cards.more: Picture a small train again. In a normal sentence the engine, brauchst, is in the front and the carriage, kommen, is at the back. Inside a dass clause the whole train turns around: the engine now sits at the very back, and the carriage with its zu comes before it. Nothing else changes: the same words, only reversed at the end. Practise it by saying the short sentence first and then adding dass in front.

rows: …, dass du nicht zu kommen brauchst.
…, dass wir nicht zu warten brauchen.

cards.title: Never alone: brauchen vs müssen
cards.body: Brauchen + zu never means must on its own. Without nicht, kein or nur you need müssen: Du musst kommen, not Du brauchst zu kommen. In speech people often drop zu: Du brauchst nicht kommen. You will hear it often, but in writing always add zu.
cards.lead: You have the pattern. This last card sets a limit: when brauchen can be used with zu, and when it cannot. It also warns you about the spoken short form.

examples.de: Du musst kommen.
examples.en: You must come.

examples.de: Du brauchst nicht zu kommen.
examples.en: You do not need to come.

examples.de: Ich brauche Hilfe.
examples.en: I need help.

deeper.text: In the past people avoid brauchen + zu, because the Perfekt sounds heavy. They say: Das war nicht nötig. Or: Du musstest nicht kommen. Ich habe nicht kommen müssen is possible but rare. Brauchen as a normal verb stays easy: Ich brauche Hilfe. Ich habe Hilfe gebraucht.

example.de: Das war nicht nötig.
example.en: That was not necessary.

cards.more: Think of two drawers. In the first drawer, brauchen is a full verb with a noun: ich brauche Hilfe, ich brauche Zeit. No zu there. In the second drawer, brauchen sits next to an infinitive and only in a no-need or only sentence, and zu goes in. Nothing in between! If a sentence says you have to, forget brauchen and take müssen. The spoken short form without zu is a habit of speech: understand it, but write the version with zu.

lessons.title: Vorsicht, heiß!: warning someone
lessons.goal: Warn someone clearly and politely, understand warning signs and tell what happened in a small accident.

grammar.point: Short warnings (Vorsicht! Pass auf!) use the imperative in du, ihr and Sie forms. Pass auf, dass … sends the verb to the end and usually contains nicht. Warnen takes vor + dative. Signs use the infinitive. Small accidents use the Perfekt: haben with a dative reflexive, sein with ausrutschen and stolpern.
grammar.oneLine: Pass auf, dass du dir nicht den Finger verbrennst!

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Mach das nicht!' to 'Pass auf, dass du dich nicht verbrennst!'
cards.body: Leon cooks for Frau Weber, and the pan is hot. A good warning is short and clear, but it can also explain what you want to avoid. Today you warn someone politely and say what happened after a small accident, with the dative pronouns from lesson 1 and 3.
steps: You already know: Sei vorsichtig! and Mach das nicht! (short commands)
New today: Pass auf, dass du dir nicht den Finger verbrennst! (a warning with a reason)
By the end you can: warn someone with du, Sie and ihr, understand warning signs and tell what happened.

examples.de: Sei vorsichtig!
examples.en: Be careful!
examples.why: You know this: a short command.

examples.de: Mach das nicht!
examples.en: Do not do that!
examples.why: You know this: a command with nicht.

examples.de: Pass auf, dass du dir nicht den Finger verbrennst!
examples.en: Be careful that you do not burn your finger!
examples.why: New today: a warning with a dass-clause.

examples.en: I warn you about the hot pan.
examples.why: New today: warnen vor + dative.

cards.more: A warning has two jobs: it must be fast, and it must be clear. For that, German has short words like Vorsicht or Achtung. When you have a second more, you add the danger: Pass auf, dass du nicht rutschst. That sentence is a command plus a reason, like a small safety rule. In a kitchen, on stairs or in a lab, friends say it all the time. You use it to care for people, not to scare them.

cards.title: Leon cooks for Frau Weber
cards.body: Leon is cooking at Frau Weber's. Mira sees the pan on the hob and the wet floor, and warns him. Notice how short the first words are: just the danger and a command. The pan and the floor give you the first vocabulary for this lesson.
cards.lead: This card is a short scene in the kitchen. Look at how Mira warns first with one word, then with a short sentence, and how Leon answers calmly.

examples.de: Vorsicht, die Pfanne ist heiß!
examples.en: Careful, the pan is hot!

examples.de: Der Boden ist nass.
examples.en: The floor is wet.

examples.de: Fass den Griff nicht an!
examples.en: Do not touch the handle!

deeper.text: In the kitchen a warning can also be a plain statement: Die Pfanne ist heiß. The listener understands it as a warning because of the tone and the situation. Mira often says the danger first and the command second, so the other person can react immediately.

example.de: Die Herdplatte ist noch heiß.
example.en: The hob is still hot.

cards.more: Picture a smoke alarm. It does not give a speech, it makes one loud sound and you move. A short warning works the same way: Vorsicht! tells the body to stop, and the second half, die Pfanne ist heiß, gives the reason. In German the order is often danger first, command second, or just the danger alone. If you only have one second, say the danger; if you have two seconds, add the command.
steps: Mira: Vorsicht, die Pfanne ist heiß!
Leon: Danke, ich passe auf.
Mira: Der Boden ist nass. Pass auf, dass du nicht ausrutschst!
Leon: Keine Sorge, ich bin vorsichtig.

cards.title: Short warnings: du, Sie, ihr
cards.body: Short warnings need no subject. Vorsicht! and Achtung! are single words. Pass auf! uses the imperative of aufpassen, a separable verb: the prefix auf goes to the end. The forms change with the person: du Pass auf!, ihr Passt auf!, Sie Passen Sie auf!
cards.lead: You know imperatives from A1. Now you use them to warn: first the one-word alarms, then the three forms of Pass auf! for the three groups of people you talk to.

examples.de: Pass auf!
examples.en: Be careful! (to du)

examples.de: Passt auf!
examples.en: Be careful! (to ihr)

examples.de: Passen Sie auf!
examples.en: Be careful! (to Sie)

deeper.text: Bloß nicht! is a very strong warning and can sound rude, because it forbids. Friends say it softer with lieber: Lass das lieber. (I would leave that.) Mach das lieber nicht. Lieber with an imperative sounds like advice, not like an order, and keeps the mood friendly.

example.de: Lass das lieber!
example.en: Better leave that!

cards.more: Think of a volume knob. Vorsicht! is the middle setting, loud enough to get attention. Achtung! is a bit louder, like a sign. Bloß nicht! is the highest setting, you turn it up only when it is really dangerous. Lass das lieber is the lowest setting, it is advice between friends. Pick the setting that fits the danger and the person. To Frau Weber and Herr Ali the four use Sie, to each other du or ihr.

rows: Passen Sie auf! / Seien Sie vorsichtig!

cards.title: Pass auf, dass …
cards.body: To say what you want to avoid, add a dass-clause. The verb goes to the end, as you know. Most often the clause has nicht and the thing you do NOT want: Pass auf, dass du nicht rutschst. With a reflexive verb the pronoun comes right after the subject: dass du dir nicht wehtust.
cards.lead: After the short alarm words, a longer sentence says what exactly can go wrong. Here you combine the imperative Pass auf with a dass-clause and use the verb at the end.

examples.de: Pass auf, dass du nicht rutschst.
examples.en: Be careful that you do not slip.

examples.de: Pass auf, dass du dir nicht wehtust.
examples.en: Be careful that you do not hurt yourself.

examples.de: Achte darauf, dass die Pfanne nicht überkocht.
examples.en: Make sure the pan does not boil over.

deeper.text: Pass auf, dass du nicht fällst has nicht in the clause, but the meaning is: do not fall. German thinks of the dangerous action and says nicht. Learners from other languages often forget the nicht and say the opposite. Compare: Pass auf, dass du fällst would mean you should fall.

example.de: Pass auf, dass du nicht fällst.
example.en: Be careful that you do not fall.

cards.more: Imagine the sentence as a small stage. The command Pass auf comes first and gets the attention. Then comes the comma, which is like a curtain, and behind it the dass-clause shows the scene you want to avoid: du, nicht, rutschst. The verb stands in the last place, like a person at the end of the line. If you forget the nicht, you ask the other person to do the dangerous thing, so always say it out loud.

cards.title: warnen vor + Dativ
cards.body: Warnen takes vor and the dative: Ich warne dich vor der heißen Pfanne. Die heiße Pfanne becomes der heißen Pfanne, because vor with the dative gives the dative. You can also say Es ist gefährlich, die Herdplatte anzufassen: es ist gefährlich with zu + infinitive, which you know from B1.
cards.lead: Besides imperatives, you can warn about a thing. This card gives the verb warnen with vor and the dative, and the structure Es ist gefährlich, … zu … for general warnings.

examples.de: Ich warne dich vor der heißen Pfanne.
examples.en: I warn you about the hot pan.

examples.de: Mira warnt Frau Weber vor dem nassen Boden.
examples.en: Mira warns Frau Weber about the wet floor.

examples.de: Es ist gefährlich, die Herdplatte anzufassen.
examples.en: It is dangerous to touch the hob.

deeper.text: Warnen vor takes a thing: Ich warne dich vor dem Hund. If you want to warn about a whole fact, use the da-word: Ich warne dich davor, dass die Pfanne heiß ist. A da-word (davor) points ahead to the dass-clause, as in B1 chapter 4. The same pattern works with Ich warne dich davor, den Boden zu betreten.

example.de: Ich warne dich davor, dass die Pfanne heiß ist.
example.en: I warn you that the pan is hot.

cards.more: Think of vor as a small shield. You hold the shield in front of the other person and say what you are protecting them from: vor der Pfanne, vor dem Boden. The thing behind vor goes into the dative: die Pfanne turns into der Pfanne, der Boden into dem Boden. If the danger is a whole sentence, you cannot put a noun behind vor, so you use davor and a dass-clause. In both cases the verb is always warnen, the shield is always vor.

rows: Ich warne dich vor der Pfanne.
Ich warne dich vor dem Boden.
Ich warne dich vor dem Messer.

cards.title: Signs and rules
cards.body: Signs speak to everyone and so use the infinitive, not du or Sie: Nicht berühren! Nicht betreten! Nicht anfassen! A sign can also name the danger as a noun: Rutschgefahr! A Warnschild often shows a picture, so it needs only one or two words.
cards.lead: In the hospital, at the cooker or on the stairs you read warning signs. Here you see what a sign says and why it uses the infinitive and not a command to one person.

examples.de: Nicht berühren!
examples.en: Do not touch!

examples.de: Nicht betreten!
examples.en: Do not enter!

examples.de: Achtung, Rutschgefahr!
examples.en: Careful, risk of slipping!

deeper.text: A sign does not know who reads it, so it chooses a form that fits everyone, the infinitive: Nicht berühren! The same trick works in a recipe: Zwiebeln schneiden, Pfanne erhitzen. For a person you know you use the imperative: Fass das nicht an!

example.de: Nicht anfassen!
example.en: Do not touch!

cards.more: Think of a street sign. It does not say Sie, it does not say du, it says only the message. German signs do the same with the verb: the infinitive without any person, and nicht at the start. If you meet a sign with a noun like Rutschgefahr, you get the whole warning in one word: the risk of slipping. You do not need to write signs yourself, but you need to read them quickly.

cards.title: What happened?
cards.body: To tell about a small accident, use the Perfekt. With a dative reflexive, the pronoun is mir, dir or sich: Leon hat sich den Finger verbrannt. Ich habe mir in den Finger geschnitten. Verbs of sudden movement take sein: Ich bin ausgerutscht. Er ist gestolpert.
cards.lead: After the warning comes the story. Here you tell what happened in the Perfekt and decide between haben with a dative reflexive and sein with a verb of movement.

examples.de: Leon hat sich den Finger verbrannt.
examples.en: Leon burned his finger.

examples.de: Ich habe mir in den Finger geschnitten.
examples.en: I cut my finger.

examples.de: Ich bin auf der Treppe ausgerutscht.
examples.en: I slipped on the stairs.

deeper.text: Ausrutschen and stolpern take sein because the person moves and suddenly ends up somewhere else. The reflexive verbs sich verbrennen and sich schneiden take haben. If you are not sure, ask: did I move somewhere? Then sein. Did I do something to a part of my body? Then haben with mir or sich.

example.de: Er ist über die Stufe gestolpert.
example.en: He tripped over the step.

cards.more: Picture a small accident as two types. In the first type, you suddenly move: you slip, you trip, you fall. These verbs say that the body changes its place, so they take sein. In the second type, you do something to a part of the body: you burn a finger, you cut a hand. There is an accusative object, the finger, so the pronoun is dative: mir, dir, sich. Together with haben, they make the Perfekt of the second type.

rows: Ich habe mir den Finger verbrannt.

cards.title: Warn without scaring
cards.body: A good warning can also calm. Say first that there is no big problem, then the danger. Keine Angst, aber … works well. So does Du brauchst nicht zu erschrecken, aber … from lesson 4: brauchen + nicht + zu. Use both in a role-play in the Kochkurs.
cards.lead: You can now warn and report. This last card combines the two: you warn without making the other person afraid, and you use the brauchen + zu pattern from lesson 4.

examples.de: Du brauchst nicht zu erschrecken, aber die Pfanne ist heiß.
examples.en: You do not need to be afraid, but the pan is hot.

examples.de: Keine Angst, aber pass auf!
examples.en: No fear, but be careful!

examples.de: Das ist nicht schlimm, aber nimm einen Verband.
examples.en: It is not bad, but take a bandage.

deeper.text: Aber after the calming phrase is the key: the first half calms and the second half gives the information. Keine Angst, aber … is friendly because it respects the other person. In the Kochkurs, the Kursleiter says to a learner with a small burn: Keine Angst, aber zeigen Sie die Hand bitte der Ärztin.

example.de: Keine Angst, aber zeigen Sie die Hand bitte der Ärztin.
example.en: No fear, but please show your hand to the doctor.

cards.more: Think of a seesaw again. On the left side goes the calm part: Keine Angst, Du brauchst nicht zu erschrecken, Das ist nicht schlimm. On the right side goes the important part: the danger or the instruction. Aber is the middle point that holds both together. A warning that has only the right side feels like a shout; one that has only the left side does not help. The mix helps people stay calm and do the right thing.

lessons.title: Das habe ich mir angewöhnt: habits
lessons.goal: Name habits and routines, say that you started or gave up a habit and read a short info text about healthy habits.

grammar.point: Sich (Dat) etwas angewöhnen and abgewöhnen take a dative pronoun and an object or a zu-clause. Sich bewegen and sich ernähren take the accusative pronoun. Die Angewohnheit + zu + infinitive and brauchen + zu are used for habits.

mistake.right: Ich habe mir angewöhnt, früh aufzustehen.
mistake.why: The zu-clause is the accusative object, so the reflexive pronoun is dative: mir.

terms.meaning: a habit you picked up, often small and sometimes slightly negative
a person who always does the same things in the same way

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich trinke jeden Morgen Kaffee' to 'Ich habe mir angewöhnt, morgens einen Spaziergang zu machen'
cards.body: At breakfast the WG talks about what everyone does every day. You can already say how often you do something. Today you say that you have made something a habit or given it up, with the dative pronoun from lesson 3 and a zu-clause.
steps: You already know: Ich trinke immer Kaffee. (a frequency word)
New today: Ich habe mir angewöhnt, früh aufzustehen. (I got into the habit of getting up early.)
By the end you can: name habits, say you started or gave one up, and talk about healthy habits.
